name: Astbury Yew
access: Free. Open churchyard of St Mary's, Astbury.
transport: Astbury is about 2 km south of Congleton, whose railway station is on the Manchester to Stoke line. Check the local bus operator for buses from the town.
story:
In 1915 a history of Astbury noted that its yew was so hollow that several people could shelter inside it at once. A century later the trunk is open enough to see straight through, and the tree leans on timber props beside the churchyard path.

It has been dated more often than it has been measured. Newbold's history computed it at least 1,000 years old. Morton put it in Saxon times. An excursion party in 1888 settled for an ancient yew of some centuries' growth. St Mary's own church page goes furthest, saying tree-ring dating suggests two thousand years. A hollow yew has lost the rings at its heart, so we give that as the parish's figure. Tim Hills of the Ancient Yew Group visited in 1999, wrote that its vast old age cannot be doubted, and left it there.

Nobody has recorded a girth either. The Group classes it as more than seven metres and unmeasurable, which is what a trunk that is mostly gap does to a tape.

In 1999 it had only one branch above about 20 feet, and one prop. By 2016 there were two. Photographs from 2007 and 2016 show plenty of green, and those are the most recent records we have, so if you visit, tell us how it looks.

It stands on the north side of St Mary's church, in a village a couple of kilometres south of Congleton.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the timber props holding up its leaning, hollow trunk, open enough to see through. It stands beside the path on the north side of St Mary's church.

name: Goostrey Yew

location.address: St Luke's churchyard, Church Bank, Goostrey, Crewe

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Luke's, Church Bank, Goostrey.
transport: Goostrey has its own railway station on the Crewe to Manchester line; check the walk to Church Bank on a map.
story:
When Goostrey rebuilt its church in the 18th century, it kept the yew. A wooden church of about 1220 gave way to the St Luke's of 1792, and the old tree by the entrance stayed where it was, as a short history of the church and its yew recorded in 1992.

It was famous already. In 1825 Hulbert's Museum Europaeum described a remarkably large yew, calculated to have stood at least a thousand years, and a letter to the Gentleman's Magazine in the 1830s gave it twelve yards round and the same thousand years. Twelve yards is 36 feet. When Tim Hills of the Ancient Yew Group measured it in 1999, he found about 25 feet close to the ground, 7.62 metres, just above the spreading roots.

What he described was a male tree whose heart has become a platform of heartwood about three feet high and four and a half across, held together by crumbling sapwood. The Group classes it as exceptional.

The parish council speaks of the village's 1,200-year-old yew, and the church says it is believed to be around 1,200 years old, with a framed certificate inside the door recording the figure. Neither says what the number rests on, so it is the parish's figure, not a measurement.

That 1999 visit is our latest firm record of the tree, so a dated photograph from you would help. It stands just beside the south entrance of St Luke's.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its low, broad trunk, a platform of old heartwood about a metre high. It stands just beside the south entrance of St Luke's church.

name: Nether Alderley Yew

location.address: St Mary's churchyard, Church Lane, Nether Alderley, Macclesfield

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Nether Alderley

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Mary's on Church Lane, opposite Nether Alderley Mill.
transport: The nearest railway station is Alderley Edge, a few kilometres away, and the A34 runs past the village. Check the local bus operator for buses.
story:
An account from 1850 found an ancient stone font standing under the old yew at St Mary's, Nether Alderley, out in the churchyard. The church's own history says the font once lay buried by the tree.

The parish calls it the 1,200-year-old yew, and the church archivist told Macclesfield Live it dates back 1,200 years. Neither says what the number rests on. The Ancient Yew Group gives it no age, only a size class of five to seven metres round, which by the Group's own reckoning usually means a tree above 500 years.

The girth is an old figure, 18 feet or about 5.5 metres, from Allen Meredith's gazetteer of 1994. Tim Hills of the Group did not measure it when he visited in 1999, but he described a male tree whose trunk holds its girth a long way up, great rolls of wood flowing round the stumps of sawn-off branches, and a hole about two and a half feet up through which a stem shows growing inside. In 1938 Notes and Queries called it a veteran with great spreading branches.

Two younger yews keep it company. One is tall and straight and may have layered from the old tree; the other has fallen and twisted. The church also points to a Saxon preaching cross in its grounds.

St Mary's is on Church Lane, opposite Nether Alderley Mill. Our latest dated record of the yew is that 1999 visit, so tell us how it looks.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the great rolls of wood round its sawn-off branches and a small hole low on the trunk with a stem inside. It stands south-south-east of St Mary's church, two younger yews beside it.

name: Farndon Yew
age_estimate: not documented (the Ancient Yew Group class puts it above 500 years)

location.address: St Chad's churchyard, High Street, Farndon, Chester

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Chad's on the High Street.
transport: No railway station. Farndon is on the River Dee about 12 km south of Chester; check the local bus operator for buses from Chester.
story:
About eight feet up its trunk, the Farndon yew has swallowed a rock some seven inches across. The Ancient Yew Group records it without saying how the stone got there.

Local legend gives the tree a part in the Civil War. Brereton's Parliamentarian troops are said to have leaned their pikes and swords against it before going into St Chad's, which served as a barracks in the war. Britain Express and the Ancient Yew Group both repeat the story. Neither cites a record from the time, so take it as the village's telling. The church was rebuilt in 1658, all but the tower.

It is a female tree near the porch on the north side. Much of its heartwood is dead and it is hollow in places, and a fluted inner stem shows where the sapwood shell of the original trunk has gone. Two recorders from the Group measured it at 20 feet 5 inches, 6.22 metres, three feet up in 2010, noted that it was undoubtedly larger once, and found a large, healthy crown.

No source gives it an age. The Group's size class puts it above 500 years, and we go no further. The site may have been in use since Anglo-Saxon times, and the outline of the present church is 14th-century.

Farndon sits on the River Dee on the Welsh border, about 12 km south of Chester. Our latest record is from 2010, so a photograph would help.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a rock about 18 centimetres across caught in its trunk, roughly eight feet up. It stands near the porch on the north side of St Chad's church.

name: Lanercost Priory Yews
age_estimate: not documented (hollow veteran, over 130 years on record)

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Lanercost Priory

access: Free. Open churchyard of Lanercost Priory; the priory ruins are an English Heritage site; check English Heritage for their opening times.
transport: No station in the village. Lanercost is a few miles from Brampton; check the local bus operator for buses.

location_site.name: Lanercost Priory churchyard (burial ground NE of the church)

story:
Half a dozen people can fit inside the leaning yew at Lanercost, through a small hole in its hollow shell, according to Ken Mills's Cumbrian Yew Book of 1999. The tree has taken hard knocks to get there. A gale in November 1891 tore away much of its crown, and when John Lowe described it a few years later it was hollow, broken at fifteen feet and forming a new head.

Since then it has hardly widened. Lowe gave it 14 feet round at three feet up in 1896 or 1897. A hundred years on, Graham Wilkinson found 14 feet 8 inches, and Tim Hills of the Ancient Yew Group 14 feet 5 inches in 2002. Taken at the ground, where the lean stretches it, the figure is 5.44 metres.

It stands in the burial ground north-east of the priory church, close beside a female yew. She has a patch of old white sapwood showing and traces at her base of a twin trunk that was lost. Wilkinson also noted another large yew to the south, near the Prior's House.

The priory ruins are in the care of English Heritage. No source gives either tree an age, and the last measurement was taken in 2002. If you visit, tell us how the pair are doing and send a photograph.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its lean and the small hole into its hollow shell, with a female yew close beside it. They stand in the burial ground north-east of the priory church.
